# Cupertino

> MCP servers for the Apple apps already on your Mac — Mail, Notes, Reminders and
> Calendar — and the signed menu-bar app that holds their one Full Disk Access grant instead of
> handing it to every editor.

Unofficial. Not affiliated with Apple. macOS 26 or later, and macOS only. Not shipped yet: the
signed app and the `@mgcrea/mcp-apple-*` packages land together at the first release.

## The argument

- Full Disk Access is a single, indivisible grant, and it lands on whatever process launched the
  server — your editor or your terminal, never Mail itself. Granting it to Mail.app does nothing.
- Four MCP hosts therefore mean four whole-disk grants. Cupertino is one signed, notarized app that
  holds it once, and the bundle identifier `io.mgcrea.cupertino` is the TCC identity, so the grant
  survives updates.
- The grant buys speed as well as reach: the same Mail search is 74,000 ms over Apple Events and
  97 ms off the Envelope Index.
- Write tools are not merely refused when writes are off — they are never registered, because MCP
  clients cache the tool list.

## Surfaces

- Mail — 18 tools (10 always registered, 8 write-gated). `@mgcrea/mcp-apple-mail`
- Notes — 12 tools (7 always registered, 5 write-gated). `@mgcrea/mcp-apple-notes`
- Reminders — 11 tools (6 always registered, 5 write-gated). `@mgcrea/mcp-apple-reminders`
- Calendar — 9 tools (6 always registered, 3 write-gated). `@mgcrea/mcp-apple-calendar`
- Messages — not started. It has no Apple Events read path, so it cannot ship without the grant.

## Price

- $14.99 once, covering every 1.x release. Not a subscription, nothing lapses, and 2.0 is a separate
  purchase. EU buyers are quoted and charged €14.99, VAT included — that is not a conversion of the
  dollar figure, which is quoted tax-exclusive. Not on sale yet — the app has not shipped.
- The ladder is published in advance and tied to shipped surfaces rather than dates: $24.99 when
  Messages lands, $34.99 when Safari does. It never goes back down.
- A 30-minute trial, started by pressing a button and never armed on its own. Every surface at full
  function, with the write toggles behaving exactly as they will after paying. It is held in memory
  and never written to disk, so quitting and reopening starts another one; nothing prevents that and
  nothing pretends to. When it closes, the servers it started are stopped — refusing only new
  connections would not close it, since an MCP host opens one stdio connection and holds it for the
  life of the editor.
- The trial answers whether Cupertino works against your mail. The 30-day refund answers whether it
  was worth the money. They are different questions and both are available.
- The servers are MIT and run on their own with no key at all. The app is a different matter: its
  source is public and readable, but any build of it — yours or ours — asks for a licence key. A
  licence buys the signed and notarized binary and the upkeep, not access to the source.
- The licence key is verified offline. There is no account, no login and no phone-home — the app
  makes no network connections at all, which is checked in CI against the built binary.
